context.en: Worn by King Gustav III of Sweden, 24 April 1778

credit.name: The National Costume
credit.author: The Royal Armoury (Livrustkammaren), Stockholm. Scan by Erik Lernestål
credit.licence: CC BY-SA 4.0 (https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/4.0/). Our optimised copy is shared under the same licence; changes are listed in scripts/models.config.json.

material.en: Pink, cream and green silk embroidery, worked with metal thread over a pale rose silk ground.

made.en: The design was embroidered onto the cut pieces before the coat was sewn up, so every flower sits exactly where an edge will fall.

artistry.en: The flowers run in one unbroken border down both fronts, framing the body like a portrait. The braided bars between the buttons keep time with them.

alt.en: Close-up of the floral embroidery beside the buttons

material.en: Silk breeches gathered into a band just below the knee and tied with ribbon.

made.en: The legs were cut full and pleated into the band, then fastened with ribbon ties rather than buckles.

artistry.en: Like the puffed shoulders, the loose, ribboned breeches look back to older Swedish dress instead of to Paris.

alt.en: Close-up of a ribbon tie at the knee

material.en: A roll of gathered silk set into the top of the sleeve.

made.en: Strips of silk were gathered into a rounded puff and stitched into the armhole seam before the sleeve went in.

artistry.en: The puff recalls the slashed sleeves of the 1500s. Gustav III wanted a costume that looked Swedish and historic, not borrowed from Versailles.

alt.en: The gathered puff at the shoulder

material.en: A silk cape lined in pale silk and edged with a broad embroidered border.

made.en: It is gathered into the neckline at the back, so it falls in deep folds from the shoulders.

artistry.en: Only seen from behind, the cape turns a close-fitting coat into a ceremonial silhouette. The same floral border as the front ties the two together.

alt.en: Sketch of the cape falling from the shoulders

title.en: The Parade Armour of King Erik XIV

context.en: Made for King Erik XIV of Sweden, around 1562

credit.name: The Parade Armour of King Erik XIV of Sweden
credit.author: The Royal Armoury (Livrustkammaren), Stockholm
credit.licence: CC BY 4.0 (https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/). Changes are listed in scripts/models.config.json.

material.en: Steel, darkened, with raised ornament that was once richly gilded.

made.en: The visor pivots on rivets at the sides of the helmet. A single slit lets the wearer see, set on a ridge so a lance point glances away.

artistry.en: Even the visor carries figures in relief, so the king's face becomes a sculpted mask.

material.en: Steel, with ornament beaten up from behind and then gilded.

made.en: The armour was probably made in Arboga, then sent to Antwerp, where the goldsmith Elisaeus Libaerts hammered the design from the back and sharpened it from the front.

artistry.en: The scenes come from ancient myth, chosen because they could be read as flattering echoes of Swedish history.

alt.en: Close-up of the relief on the breastplate

material.en: Overlapping steel plates guard the shoulder, each riveted so it can slide over the next.

made.en: The curved plates overlap like roof tiles and are joined with rivets that move in slots, so the arm can still rise.

artistry.en: The lion is Sweden's heraldic beast. On the shoulder it is seen from the side, as the king rode past.

alt.en: The lion in relief on the shoulder plate

material.en: The back is decorated in the same gilded relief as the front.

made.en: Front and back plates are joined at the shoulders and sides by straps and buckles, so attendants could arm the king.

artistry.en: Parade armour was made to be seen from every side. In a procession through Stockholm, the crowd saw the king's back as often as his face.
